claims.text: The material family is Fe-Co-Ni-based fcc high-entropy alloys, including CoCrFeMnNi.
The orbital moment contribution to magnetic-entropy-related stacking fault energy is negligible in the baseline alloy.
Similarity between the fcc and hcp magnetic states reduces the magnetic entropy contribution to stacking fault energy.
Creating an fcc-hcp magnetic moment difference greater than 0.1 μ_B will make the orbital moment contribution significant and non-canceling.
The initial material may be polycrystalline or single-crystalline.
Longitudinal spin fluctuations induce magnetic moments that are similar in the fcc and hcp phases of CoCrFeMnNi.
Short-range chemical ordering, precipitate formation, or uniaxial strain can decouple the fcc and hcp magnetic moments.
The intervention can produce a magnetic moment difference greater than 0.1 μ_B for Fe, Mn, or Co.
The relevant calculations use first-principles DFT with longitudinal spin fluctuations over 300–1200 K and multiple volumes.
The modeled volumes include deliberately strained states.
The relevant structural mediator is the fcc-hcp difference in spin and orbital magnetic moments.
The baseline fcc-hcp magnetic moment difference is less than 0.005 μ_B.
Nearly identical fcc and hcp magnetic states cause magnetic terms to cancel in the stacking fault energy calculation.
A sufficiently large phase-dependent magnetic moment disparity will break the cancellation and make the orbital contribution dominant in the total stacking fault energy.
The intervention will increase the magnetic entropy contribution to stacking fault energy by more than 10 mJ m^-2 relative to baseline.
The predicted stacking fault energy change will measurably shift the critical fcc-to-hcp transformation temperature.
The predicted stacking fault energy change will alter strain-hardening behavior.
Including longitudinal spin fluctuations changes stacking fault energy by approximately 13.5 mJ m^-2 in the most fcc-stable region.
The approximately 13.5 mJ m^-2 change specifically represents a minimal magnetic entropy contribution relative to non-magnetic models.
Current simulations cannot readily isolate the orbital moment contribution from the spin moment contribution.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and intervention use Δm > 0.1 μ_B as a meaningful threshold for producing a significant orbital contribution, while the uncertainty field states that the threshold separating negligible from dominant behavior is not quantified.

The less-than-0.005 μ_B fcc-hcp difference is phrased as a general baseline value, although the cited basis applies specifically to Ni; the evidence reports substantially larger differences for Co, Cr, Fe, and Mn at 100 K.
